content:
Your first gifts may arrive before your first public service. Decide how you will record and acknowledge them before a donor asks for a statement at tax time.

A clear receipt tells a donor what your church received and what, if anything, you provided in return. This guide covers U.S. federal receipt rules and a practical statement process. A receipt does not establish that every donor can deduct a gift. Leave the donor's tax return to the donor and their tax adviser.

---

## Assign the receipt process

Ask your Financial Leader to name the person who prepares receipts and another authorized person who reviews them. Follow your existing separation of duties. Keep individual giving records with those who need them for financial work; the Senior Pastor should not prepare donor statements or receive individual giving totals.

Use your church's accounting or giving system for this work. Establish a contact address for corrections and keep a copy of every statement you send. If a sending church receives gifts for your plant, agree with its Financial Leader about which organization acknowledges those gifts. Do not have both organizations issue receipts that describe the same donor payment as a gift received by each.

---

## Know which rule applies

The IRS distinguishes the donor's records from the charity's disclosure duties.

| Situation | What to provide or explain |
|---|---|
| Monetary gift of any amount | The donor needs a bank record or church communication showing the organization's name, gift date and amount. |
| Single contribution of $250 or more | The donor needs a timely written acknowledgment from the receiving charity, including the goods-or-services statement. |
| Payment over $75, partly a gift and partly for goods or services | The charity must give a written disclosure of the benefit's estimated value and the limit on the deductible portion, unless an exception applies. |

Apply the $250 test to each contribution. Several smaller gifts do not become a single contribution because their annual total is $250 or more. Still offer every identified donor an accurate statement.

<Callout type="important">
Federal guidance checked October 15, 2026. Before issuing statements, confirm the current $250 acknowledgment and over-$75 disclosure thresholds with the IRS, using Publication 1771 and its charitable contribution guidance. Ask your accountant about rules for the gift year you are reporting.
</Callout>

---

## Include the acknowledgment details

Use the receiving organization's name. Include the donor's name and the date and amount of each monetary gift. For donated property, describe the property without assigning its tax value.

Address what the donor received in exchange. State that you provided no goods or services if that is true. Otherwise, describe the goods or services and give a good faith estimate of their value. If the only return was intangible religious benefits, say so instead.

Intangible religious benefits include admission to a religious ceremony and generally are not sold commercially outside a gift context. They do not include consumer goods, travel services or education leading to a recognized degree. Have your accountant check wording when the distinction is unclear.

For an ordinary monetary gift with nothing provided in return, a receipt could read:

> Riverbend Church acknowledges a monetary gift of $320 from Jordan Lee on October 4, 2026. The church provided no goods or services in exchange for this gift.

Use wording that matches the actual transaction. Add your contact information so the donor can report an error.

---

## Send it while it can help

A donor must obtain the acknowledgment by the earlier of the date they file their original return for the gift year or that return's due date, including extensions. An acknowledgment sent after the donor files may be too late.

Send acknowledgments promptly throughout the year. A single annual statement can cover several qualifying gifts. List the individual dates and amounts, and include the required acknowledgment language. A paper letter or an email can serve as written acknowledgment.

Use January 31 after the gift year as an internal delivery target, and honor earlier requests. Publication 1771 describes that date as typical charity practice. The controlling deadline for the donor is the earlier-of rule above.

<Callout type="tip">
Send a sample statement to your reviewer before the year ends. Check the organization's name, individual gift entries and acknowledgment language, then test how the donor will open and save it.
</Callout>

---

## Disclose goods and services

A fundraising meal or item offered in return for a payment needs separate attention. The over-$75 disclosure test uses the whole payment, including the benefit's value.

For example, suppose someone pays $120 at a fundraiser and receives a meal with a fair market value of $35. The potential charitable portion is $85. Your written disclosure must explain that only the payment exceeding the benefit's value may be deductible and give the $35 good faith estimate. These figures illustrate the calculation; they are not IRS thresholds.

Provide the disclosure when soliciting or receiving the payment. Do not postpone it until the annual statement. Keep the basis for your valuation with the event records.

<Callout type="warning">
Do not put a blanket no-goods-or-services statement on fundraiser payments when donors received a benefit. Exceptions exist for certain small benefits and intangible religious benefits. Confirm an exception before relying on it; the IRS adjusts some small-benefit limits for inflation.
</Callout>

---

## Handle unusual gifts separately

For donated equipment, acknowledge the item and receipt date, and address any goods or services provided in return. Keep the property description separate from the monetary gift total. The donor handles valuation and any required appraisal. An authorized church signature on Form 8283 acknowledges receipt; it does not endorse the donor's appraised value.

Volunteer time and services are not deductible contributions. Thank volunteers without assigning a deductible amount to their hours. Certain unreimbursed expenses may qualify under separate rules. Have your accountant review the acknowledgment needed for those expenses.

Refer vehicles, securities, retirement-account distributions and gifts through a donor-advised fund for review before applying your ordinary receipt template. This guide does not supply their specialized tax documentation.

---

## Prepare the annual statement

Before sending statements:

- [ ] Reconcile recorded gifts with counting, deposit and online payment records.
- [ ] Review duplicate donor records and confirm the intended recipient and delivery address.
- [ ] Resolve returned payments and unexplained differences before stating a total.
- [ ] List each monetary contribution's date and amount, then verify the annual total.
- [ ] Separate property gifts and payments involving benefits from ordinary monetary gifts.
- [ ] Check acknowledgment wording against what each donor actually received.
- [ ] Have the authorized reviewer check the statements and keep the approved copies.
- [ ] Send statements privately, record delivery and follow up on failed emails or returned mail.

Keep pledges separate from gifts actually made. For year-end transactions, use the IRS contribution-timing rules rather than assigning every gift the date it reached your bank. Ask your accountant to resolve uncertain dates.

---

## Correct mistakes openly

Give donors a named contact for questions. Compare a disputed entry with the underlying records. Explain the correction, send a clearly dated replacement and retain the earlier version with the reason for changing it. Do not backdate a receipt or promise that a late correction will repair the donor's tax position.

Common mistakes include counting a pledge as a payment, sending one donor another donor's statement, omitting acknowledgment language and describing an annual total without individual gift details. Review these points before each statement run.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"In this case, moreover, it is required of stewards that one be found faithful."* — 1 Corinthians 4:2 (LSB)
</Callout>
excerpt: Set up donor acknowledgments, distinguish IRS receipt rules and prepare accurate annual giving statements for your church.
title: Donor Receipts and Giving Statements

sources.claim: Sections 2, 4 and 5. The $250 test is per contribution; annual summaries and electronic acknowledgments are allowed; January 31 is typical practice, not the controlling deadline. Some small-benefit dollar limits adjust annually. Publication 1771 revision November 2023, retrieved 2026-10-15.
sources.quote: Separate contributions of less than $250 will not be aggregated.

sources.claim: Sections 6 and 7. Volunteer time/services are not deductible, while qualifying unreimbursed expenses may be. Contribution timing differs from deposit timing; mailed checks and credit-card gifts have specific rules. Special gifts need separate review. Publication 526 is the 2025 edition accessed 2026-10-15; no donor deduction ceilings or 2026 eligibility claims are included.
sources.quote: You can’t deduct the value of your time or services

sources.claim: Section 3 and the ordinary-gift illustration. Acknowledgment includes organization name, monetary amount or property description without value, and truthful goods/services or intangible religious benefits language. Donor name/date are included as practical identifying details; Topic 506 supports date for monetary written records.
sources.quote: description (but not value) of non-cash contribution

sources.claim: Section 5. Payments partly gifts and partly purchases over $75 require disclosure based on the whole payment, an estimate of the benefit value and explanation of the deductible excess. Disclosure accompanies solicitation or receipt. The $120/$35/$85 example is original arithmetic applying this rule. Section 3 religious-benefit definition/exclusions and section 5 exceptions follow this page.
sources.quote: The charity must furnish the statement in connection with either the solicitation or the receipt

sources.claim: Section 4. The donor obtains acknowledgment by the earlier of original return filing or the due date including extensions. Donor bears responsibility for requesting and obtaining it. Section 8 late corrections therefore cannot be promised to cure a tax problem.
sources.quote: The donor is responsible for requesting and obtaining the written acknowledgement

sources.claim: Sections 2 and 3. Monetary gifts of every amount require bank records or written charity communication identifying organization, date and amount. Qualified organizations alone receive deductible contributions; receipts do not guarantee donor eligibility. One document can satisfy monetary-record and $250 acknowledgment requirements.
sources.quote: Only qualified organizations are eligible to receive tax deductible contributions

sources.claim: Section 6. Noncash gifts may need additional documentation; a donee acknowledgment signature on Form 8283 does not agree with the appraised value. Vehicle gifts can have special rules. No appraisal or form filing thresholds are taught here.
sources.quote: The signature does not represent agreement with the appraised value

sources.claim: Section 8 scripture callout. Exact full 1 Corinthians 4:2 text checked by one-verse lookup on 2026-10-15. Browser text retrieval failed; fetched the single-verse URL directly, inspected the rendered verse HTML and excluded footnote marker 1.
sources.publisher: Legacy Standard Bible / The Lockman Foundation
sources.quote: In this case, moreover, it is required of stewards that one be found faithful.

rulings: 2026-10-15: Use phase 0 because A8 omits phase and the administrative/financial section and its six published articles use phase 0. Append at sort order 7.

2026-10-15: U.S. federal receipt procedure only. Delivery, reconciliation, review and correction checklists are recommended workflow, not additional IRS mandates. No state law, retention period, donor eligibility/ceiling or specialized gift documentation is asserted.

2026-10-15: Keep the existing Financial Leader, separated duties and Senior Pastor confidentiality rules from the Playbook Accounting section and related published financial articles. No new financial or pastoral methodology. The sending-church paragraph recommends agreement on the actual receiving entity, without deciding sponsorship legal arrangements.

2026-10-15: January 31 is an internal delivery target based on Publication 1771 typical practice. State the earlier-of donor deadline separately. Use all identified donors for statement service without treating aggregated gifts as the $250 trigger.

2026-10-15: Scripture repeats the reference already used in Principles of Financial Accountability, using the individually verified full LSB verse without a new theological interpretation. The preview footer retains the full LSB notice.

2026-10-15: Eight external primary source URLs. Thresholds, disclosure duties, benefit exceptions, acknowledgment contents and timing checked as of 2026-10-15. Publication 1771 is Rev. 11-2023; Publication 526 is 2025. Omit annually indexed token amounts and deduction limits, fees, penalty amounts, specialist filing deadlines and gift-specific form thresholds.
